ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: To stand with one’s head against heaven and feet on earth is the record’s epithet for a person presented as fully standing on their own. Masters apply it to the person within a monastery’s scene, to traveling monks carrying staffs, and to the one who can withstand direct testing without retreating into excuses.
EvidenceBody: Feiyin Tongrong answers “what is the person within Huangbo’s scene?” with “head against heaven and feet on earth,” making the phrase a direct portrait-answer.
Lianfeng Su addresses the “superior one who investigates Chan” as iron-headed, copper-browed, and standing between heaven and earth before describing blows and reversals that do not move him.

Sanyi Mingyu pairs the phrase with having neither a tile overhead nor room below for an awl, while an unnamed monk in Lingji Xingguan’s record uses it to challenge why so many people are buried alive.

Juelang Daosheng makes the status conditional: only one who can pass through the successive shouts is allowed to be such a person. The phrase is therefore an epithet tested in public speech, not a physical measurement.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: The bodily posture becomes a Chan epithet for a publicly answerable, independently standing person, then appears inside direct tests of that standing.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The corpus also uses the idiom as broad praise; this entry limits its Chan claim to explicit addresses, answers, and tests in masters’ records.

ComparedThings: to stand with one’s head against heaven and feet on earth
The epithet addresses monks, answers who the person in Huangbo’s scene is, and conditionally names one who passes a test
DifferentThingTest.Reason: The epithet addresses monks, answers who the person in Huangbo’s scene is, and conditionally names one who passes a test. All picture the same heaven-high, earth-planted person.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: Stand, heaven, earth, head, feet, towering, and Chan person reproduce the bodily picture and its explicit human referent.

ModifierControls.reason: 頂 and 立 remain coordinated bodily actions with 天 and 地 as their limits; occurrences merely containing 頂天 or 立地 outside the four-graph idiom were excluded.

FamilyControls.reason: 大丈夫漢 and 漢子 identify the person receiving the epithet, while 鐵額銅頭 supplies a neighboring bodily description; neither is folded into the preferred target.
